title: Finite etale local factors lift from formal monoid coefficients
statement: Let $(E,\mathfrak n)$ be a nonzero complete regular Noetherian local commutative ring [def-weil-regular-scheme, def-weil-pbc-noetherian-ring, def-weil-pbc-adic-completion], let $S$ be a fine saturated monoid [def-trf-fs-log-blowup] which is sharp, meaning that $0$ is its only invertible element, and put $H=E[[S]]$, the completion at $(\mathfrak n,[s]:s\ne0)$ of the monoid ring $E[S]$, which has $E$-basis $[s]$ ($s\in S$) and multiplication $[s][s']=[s+s']$. Let $f$ belong to the maximal ideal of $H$, allowing $f=0$, and put $A_0=H/(f)$. Let $K$ be a nonzero local finite etale $A_0$-algebra; finite etale means finite as a module and etale on affine spectra [def-weil-finitely-generated-module, def-weil-etale-morphism, def-weil-affine-spectrum]. Then there exist a nonzero complete regular Noetherian local finite etale $E$-algebra $D$ with residue field $\kappa(K)$ and a continuous $A_0$-algebra isomorphism $K\cong D[[S]]/(f)$, where $f$ on the right is its coefficientwise image. Moreover $\mathfrak m_D=\mathfrak nD$, and the image in $D$ of every element of $\mathfrak n\setminus\mathfrak n^2$ lies in $\mathfrak m_D\setminus\mathfrak m_D^2$.

source.place: Stacks Tags 09ZL (more-algebra, lemma-finite-etale-equivalence), 07NF (algebra, lemma-regular-goes-up), 031B (algebra, lemma-when-finite-module-complete-over-complete-ring); formal monoid coefficient base-change consequence used in ILO VI 2.3.

proof.text: Put $k=E/\mathfrak n$, $R=E[S]$ and $\mathfrak b=(\mathfrak n,[s]:s\ne0)\subset R$. Sharpness implies that a sum of nonzero monoid elements cannot be zero, so sending every nonzero monomial to zero defines the augmentation $R\to E$. Thus $R/\mathfrak b=k$. Choose finitely many nonzero generators of $S$; their monomials, together with generators of $\mathfrak n$, generate $\mathfrak b$. Also $R$ is a quotient of a polynomial ring in finitely many variables over $E$, hence is Noetherian by finite-type permanence. Its completion $H$ is Noetherian by completion permanence. The completion-mod-ideal theorem gives that $H$ is complete for $\mathfrak bH$ and that $H/\mathfrak bH=k$.

Every $z\in\mathfrak bH$ is topologically nilpotent, so the compatible partial sums $1+z+\cdots+z^{q-1}$ define an inverse of $1-z$ in the complete ring $H$. If $h$ has nonzero image in the field $H/\mathfrak bH=k$, choose $v$ with $hv\equiv1\pmod{\mathfrak bH}$; the preceding inverse makes $h$ a unit. Therefore $H$ is nonzero local with maximal ideal $\mathfrak bH$ and residue field $k$. Since $f$ is in this maximal ideal, $(f)$ is proper. The complete-local quotient theorem makes $A_0=H/(f)$ a nonzero complete Noetherian local ring with maximal ideal $\mathfrak m_0=\mathfrak bH/(f)$ and residue field $k$. Completeness makes both $(E,\mathfrak n)$ and $(A_0,\mathfrak m_0)$ henselian pairs, hence henselian local rings.

source.place: Algebra Tag 0325 (lemma-quotient-complete-local); More on Algebra Tag 0ALJ (lemma-complete-henselian). The geometric-series argument is written out.

proof.text: Let $\mathfrak q$ be the maximal ideal of $K$. Since $K$ is finite over $A_0$, the finite-algebra integrality theorem and contraction of maximal ideals under integral maps give $\mathfrak q\cap A_0=\mathfrak m_0$. Apply the etale prime-ideal theorem at $\mathfrak q$. As localization of a local ring at its maximal ideal is the ring itself, it yields $\mathfrak q=\mathfrak m_0K$. The etale residue-field theorem gives that $L=K/\mathfrak q=\kappa(K)$ is finite separable over $k$. Thus $L$ is a nonzero finite etale $k$-algebra by the finite-separable-extension theorem.

Apply essential surjectivity of the henselian finite-etale equivalence to $E$ and the finite etale $k$-algebra $L$. It supplies a finite etale $E$-algebra $D$ with a fixed $k$-algebra isomorphism $D/\mathfrak nD\cong L$. This makes $D$ nonzero. The finite-algebra integrality theorem shows that every maximal ideal of $D$ contracts to the unique maximal ideal $\mathfrak n$ of $E$. Consequently every maximal ideal of $D$ contains $\mathfrak nD$; since the quotient is a field, $\mathfrak nD$ is the unique maximal ideal. Thus $D$ is local and $\mathfrak m_D=\mathfrak nD$, with residue field identified with $L$. A finite module algebra is finite type: a finite set of module generators also generates the algebra. Finite-type permanence makes $D$ Noetherian. The finite-module completeness theorem over the complete Noetherian ring $E$ makes $D$ complete for $\mathfrak nD=\mathfrak m_D$.

The regular-local localization theorem makes $E$ a regular ring. The affine etale comparison identifies $E\to D$ with a finitely presented ring map having $H_1(L_{D/E})=0$ and $\Omega_{D/E}=0$. The zero module is finite projective (a direct summand of the rank-zero free module), so the definition of a smooth ring map makes $E\to D$ smooth. Regularity ascends along smooth ring maps. Therefore $D$ is regular, and its localization at its unique maximal ideal, which is $D$ itself, is a regular local ring.

The etale-flatness theorem makes $D$ flat over $E$. Since it is finite and $E$ is local, the finite-flat-local theorem makes $D$ free over $E$. Its basis can be taken finite: the union of the finite supports of any finite generating set contains every basis vector. Fix such a basis $d_1,\ldots,d_r$; $r>0$ because $D\ne0$.

Put $R_D=D[S]$ and $\mathfrak b_D=(\mathfrak m_D,[s]:s\ne0)$. Since $\mathfrak m_D=\mathfrak nD$, one has $\mathfrak b_D=\mathfrak bR_D$. The chosen basis gives $R_D=\bigoplus_{i=1}^r d_iR$ and, for every $q\ge1$, $\mathfrak b_D^q=\bigoplus_{i=1}^r d_i\mathfrak b^q$: expand elements in the basis and multiply by the generators of the extended ideal. Hence $R_D/\mathfrak b_D^q=\bigoplus_i d_i(R/\mathfrak b^q)$. A compatible sequence in this finite direct sum is exactly $r$ compatible coordinate sequences. Taking the defining inverse limits therefore identifies $D[[S]]$ with $\bigoplus_i d_iH$. The resulting map $\Phi:D\otimes_E H\to D[[S]]$ sends $d\otimes h$ to the product of the constant coefficient $d$ and the image of $h$. It is bijective by the displayed basis calculation and multiplicative because it is induced by the commuting coefficient and monoid maps at every quotient level. Thus $\Phi$ is a ring isomorphism. In particular the image of $h\in H$ is its coefficientwise image. This calculation also works when $S=\{0\}$.

source.place: Elementary finite-basis computation from the defining inverse limits; compatible with Tag 00MA (lemma-completion-tensor).

proof.text: Under $\Phi$, multiplication by the coefficientwise image of $f$ acts as multiplication by $f$ in each of the $r$ coordinates $H$. Thus quotienting gives an $A_0$-algebra isomorphism $C:=D\otimes_E A_0\cong D[[S]]/(f)$: both modules are $\bigoplus_i d_i(H/(f))$, and their ring operations are induced by the same coefficient products in $D$ and multiplication in $H$. Explicitly the map is $d\otimes\bar h\mapsto\overline{\Phi(d\otimes h)}$, independent of the chosen lift $h$ since two lifts differ by a multiple of $f$. The inverse is given coordinatewise in the basis.

source.place: Elementary quotient and finite-basis calculation; no commutation of an infinite tensor product with a limit is assumed.

proof.text: The base-change theorem makes $C=D\otimes_E A_0$ etale over $A_0$, and its displayed $r$-element basis makes it finite. Reducing this basis presentation modulo $\mathfrak m_0$, or just sending $d\otimes a$ to $\bar a\,\bar d$, gives $C/\mathfrak m_0C\cong D\otimes_E k=D/\mathfrak nD\cong L$. Step 3 identifies $K/\mathfrak m_0K$ with the same $L$, compatibly as $k$-algebras. Full faithfulness of the henselian finite-etale equivalence for $A_0$ lifts this residue-algebra isomorphism to an $A_0$-algebra isomorphism $C\cong K$: lift the map and its inverse, and use faithfulness to see that their composites are identities. Composing its inverse with Step 8 gives the required $K\cong D[[S]]/(f)$.

source.place: Tag 00U2 (lemma-etale), base-change assertion; Tag 04GK (lemma-henselian-cat-finite-etale), full faithfulness (equivalently More on Algebra Tag 09ZL).

proof.text: The topology on $D[[S]]$ is its $\mathfrak b_DD[[S]]$-adic topology by completion-mod-ideal, since $\mathfrak m_D$ and $S$ are finitely generated and hence so is $\mathfrak b_D$. Its quotient by that ideal is $D/\mathfrak m_D=L$; the geometric-series argument of Step 2 shows that this ideal is the unique maximal ideal. The image of $f$ belongs to it. Thus on $D[[S]]/(f)$ the quotient adic topology is the maximal-ideal topology, because its defining ideal is the image of $\mathfrak b_DD[[S]]$. The algebra isomorphism from Step 9 identifies maximal ideals and all their powers. It and its inverse are therefore continuous for the maximal-ideal topologies, including the finite-algebra topology on $K$, whose defining ideal is $\mathfrak m_0K=\mathfrak q$.

source.place: Tag 05GG (lemma-hathat-finitely-generated); explicit geometric-series and ideal-power calculation.

proof.text: Finally $E\to D$ is a local flat homomorphism: it is flat by Step 6 and $\mathfrak m_D=\mathfrak nD$ by Step 4. The flat-local theorem makes it faithfully flat. Apply faithful-flat ideal contraction to $\mathfrak n^2$. If $x\in\mathfrak n\setminus\mathfrak n^2$ had image in $\mathfrak m_D^2=(\mathfrak nD)^2=\mathfrak n^2D$, contraction would give $x\in\mathfrak n^2$, a contradiction. Its image is already in $\mathfrak m_D$, proving the final assertion. When $\mathfrak n=0$ the assertion is vacuous. None of these arguments requires $f\ne0$.
